title: Algorithm Analysis and Computational Complexity
description: Asymptotic notation, analyzing loops and recursions, amortized analysis, and the classes P and NP.
overview: Two programs can solve the same problem, one in a second and one in a year. The difference is rarely the programming language or the machine; it is the algorithm and how its cost grows with the size of the input. Algorithm analysis gives a language for that growth, so that we can predict how a method will behave on ten times more data, before running it.

This chapter introduces the model of computation, big-O notation, the standard techniques for analyzing loops and recursive algorithms, amortized analysis, and the classes P and NP that separate problems we can solve efficiently from those we believe we cannot. The costs of the methods in the Machine Learning book (k-nearest neighbors, kernel methods, attention, tree building) are all stated in this language.
objectives: Count the basic operations of an algorithm and express its running time as a function of input size.
Define and use O, Ω and Θ, and compare growth rates.
Analyze nested loops and solve recurrences by the recursion tree and the master theorem.
Perform an amortized analysis of a dynamic array.
Distinguish P, NP and NP-completeness, and state the consequences for machine learning.

sections.title: Measuring cost
body: To compare algorithms independently of hardware, we count **basic operations** (arithmetic, comparisons, assignments, memory accesses) in an idealized machine, the **RAM model**, where each takes one unit of time. The **running time** T(n) is the number of operations as a function of the **input size** n: the length of a list, the number of examples, the number of bits of a number.

body: The same algorithm can behave differently on different inputs of the same size. We usually report:

list: the **worst case**, the maximum over all inputs of size n (a guarantee; here n comparisons, when the target is last or absent),
the **best case** (here 1; usually uninformative),
the **average case** under an assumption about the input distribution (here about n/2 if the target is equally likely to be anywhere).
**Space complexity** counts the memory used, besides the input.

body: Exact counts depend on details (how many operations is one comparison?) and on machine constants. For growth, only the shape matters: doubling n roughly doubles the work of linear search and quadruples the work of an algorithm that compares all pairs.

sections.title: Asymptotic notation
body: Asymptotic notation describes the growth of a function for large n, ignoring constant factors and lower-order terms.

list: **f(n) = O(g(n))** (an upper bound): there are constants c > 0 and n₀ such that f(n) ≤ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀.
**f(n) = Ω(g(n))** (a lower bound): f(n) ≥ c·g(n) for all n ≥ n₀.
**f(n) = Θ(g(n))** (a tight bound): both, so f grows exactly like g up to constants.

example.title: Dropping constants and lower-order terms
example.solution: For n ≥ 1: 3n² + 5n + 2 ≤ 3n² + 5n² + 2n² = 10n², so it is O(n²) with c = 10. Also 3n² + 5n + 2 ≥ 3n², so it is Ω(n²) with c = 3. Hence Θ(n²). The dominant term decides.

list: Logarithm bases do not matter inside O(): log₂ n and ln n differ by a constant factor.
Polynomial time, O(nᵏ), is the standard notion of 'efficient'. Exponential time is infeasible beyond small n.
O is an upper bound only: saying an algorithm is O(n²) does not say it is slow, only that it is not worse. Use Θ when you mean 'exactly'.
Constants do matter in practice. An O(n log n) algorithm with a large constant can lose to an O(n²) algorithm for small n, which is why library sorts switch to insertion sort for short arrays.

sections.title: Analyzing loops and recursion
body: Multiply the cost of the body by the number of iterations, and add sequential parts. A loop that halves the problem each time runs about log₂ n times. A double loop over pairs i < j runs Σ_{i=1}^{n} (n − i) = n(n − 1)/2 = Θ(n²) times (see the sum of integers in Discrete Mathematics).

body.caption: A quadratic double loop and a logarithmic loop.

body: A recursive algorithm's running time satisfies a **recurrence** that describes the cost on size n in terms of the cost on smaller sizes. Merge sort splits the input in two, sorts each half recursively and merges them in linear time:

Draw the **recursion tree**. Level k has 2ᵏ subproblems of size n/2ᵏ, each costing c·n/2ᵏ, so every level costs cn in total. There are log₂ n + 1 levels. The total is cn(log₂ n + 1) = Θ(n log n). For n = 1024 (10 levels of merging) with c = 1 this is about 11,264 operations, against n²/2 ≈ 524,000 for a quadratic sort.

body.key: **Master theorem.** For T(n) = aT(n/b) + Θ(nᵈ) with a ≥ 1, b > 1: if d < log_b a then T(n) = Θ(n^{log_b a}); if d = log_b a then T(n) = Θ(nᵈ log n); if d > log_b a then T(n) = Θ(nᵈ). The three cases say whether the leaves, every level equally, or the root dominates the cost.

body: The master theorem does not cover recurrences such as T(n) = T(n − 1) + T(n − 2) of the naive Fibonacci function, which recomputes the same values again and again; dynamic programming (see Dynamic Programming and Greedy Algorithms) reduces it to O(n).

check.why: a = 4, b = 2, d = 1 < log₂ 4 = 2, so the leaves dominate: n^{log_b a} = n².

sections.title: Amortized analysis
body: Some operations are usually cheap and occasionally expensive. The worst case of a single operation then overstates the cost of a long sequence. **Amortized analysis** bounds the average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence.

The classic example is the **dynamic array** (Python's list, C++'s vector). It stores items in a fixed block of memory. When the block is full, it allocates a new block of twice the size and copies everything over. Appending to a full array of n items costs n copies, but that is rare.

example.title: Amortized cost of append
example.problem: Show that n appends to an initially empty dynamic array with doubling cost O(n) in total.
solution: Each append writes one item: n writes in all. Copying happens when the array grows from size 1, 2, 4, …, up to at most n, so the total number of items copied is 1 + 2 + 4 + … + 2^{⌊log₂ n⌋} < 2n (a geometric series).
The total is less than n + 2n = 3n operations, so the **amortized cost** per append is at most 3 = O(1), though one append can cost Θ(n).

list: The doubling factor matters. If the array grew by a fixed amount (say 10 items) each time, the copying cost would be 10 + 20 + … = Θ(n²/10) and each append would cost Θ(n) amortized. Growth by a constant factor gives the geometric series.
Hash tables resize in the same way, which is why insertions are O(1) amortized.
The same idea appears in the **accounting method** (each cheap operation pays a small credit toward the expensive one) and the **potential method**.
In machine learning, the cost of training is typically stated per epoch or amortized over a mini-batch, and one-time costs such as building an index are amortized over many queries.

sections.title: Hard problems: P, NP and beyond
body: Some problems have efficient algorithms, and for others none is known. Complexity theory classifies them by the best possible running time.

list: **P** is the class of decision problems (yes/no questions) solvable in polynomial time. Sorting, shortest paths, linear programming and matrix multiplication are in P.

**NP** is the class of decision problems whose yes-answers can be //checked// in polynomial time given a certificate (a proposed solution). Does this graph have a route visiting every city with total length at most L? Given a route, checking is easy. Finding it seems to require trying exponentially many. Every problem in P is in NP.

A problem is **NP-hard** if every problem in NP reduces to it in polynomial time, and **NP-complete** if it is also in NP. If any NP-complete problem had a polynomial algorithm, all of NP would, so P = NP. Whether P = NP is the main open problem of the field; most researchers believe the answer is no.

example.title: Easy to check, hard to find
example.problem: A Boolean formula (x₁ ∨ ¬x₂) ∧ (¬x₁ ∨ x₃) ∧ (x₂ ∨ ¬x₃) is given. How hard is it to check a proposed assignment versus to find one?
example.solution: Checking the assignment (x₁, x₂, x₃) = (T, T, T): the first clause is true (x₁), the second is true (x₃), the third is true (x₂). Checking takes time linear in the formula. Finding one by brute force tries up to 2ⁿ assignments for n variables: 2⁵⁰ ≈ 10¹⁵ is already out of reach. Satisfiability (SAT) is the first problem shown to be NP-complete (Cook, 1971), and it is nonetheless solved routinely in practice for many structured instances by modern solvers.

body.h: Why it matters for machine learning

list: Many natural learning problems are NP-hard in the worst case: finding the best k-means clustering, the smallest decision tree, the best subset of features, training even a small neural network to zero error, and exact inference in general graphical models.

This does not make machine learning impossible. We use **heuristics** (greedy tree growing, Lloyd's algorithm, gradient descent) that run quickly and give good, not provably optimal, answers, and **convex relaxations** (the lasso replaces the NP-hard best-subset selection by an L1 penalty, and the hinge loss replaces the 0–1 loss).
**Approximation algorithms** guarantee a solution within a known factor of the optimum (k-means++ gives an O(log k)-approximation).
When a problem is proven NP-hard, stop looking for an exact efficient algorithm, and ask what restricted version, which approximation or which heuristic is acceptable.

body.note: Not all hard problems are in NP. Some are undecidable: no algorithm can solve them for all inputs. The halting problem (does this program terminate?) is the classic example, by a diagonal argument of Turing (1936). It implies that general program verification is impossible, and it separates what can be computed from what cannot.

summary: Running time T(n) counts basic operations in the RAM model as a function of input size, usually the worst case. Space complexity counts memory.

O, Ω and Θ give upper, lower and tight bounds ignoring constants and lower-order terms. The ladder: 1, log n, n, n log n, n², n³, 2ⁿ. At 10⁹ operations per second, n² on a million items takes 17 minutes, and exponential algorithms are hopeless beyond n ≈ 50.
Analyze loops by multiplying and adding. Solve divide-and-conquer recurrences with the recursion tree or the master theorem: T(n) = aT(n/b) + nᵈ. Merge sort is Θ(n log n); binary search is Θ(log n).
Amortized analysis averages expensive rare operations over sequences: a doubling dynamic array has O(1) amortized append.

P is efficiently solvable, NP is efficiently checkable. NP-complete problems (SAT, travelling salesman) are believed intractable. Many learning problems are NP-hard, and practice uses heuristics, relaxations and approximations.

problems.q: Give the running time in Θ-notation of: for i in range(n): for j in range(n): for k in range(j): ... (constant work in the body).
problems.solution: For each i (n values) and each j, the inner loop runs j times: Σ_j j = n(n − 1)/2. Total n · n(n − 1)/2 = Θ(n³).

problems.q: Solve T(n) = 2T(n/2) + n² with the master theorem and explain which term dominates.
problems.solution: a = 2, b = 2, d = 2. log_b a = 1 < d, so the root dominates: T(n) = Θ(n²).
problems.a: Θ(n²); the work at the root dominates.

problems.q: An algorithm takes 2 seconds on an input of size 10⁴. Estimate the time for 10⁵ if its complexity is O(n), O(n log n) and O(n²).
problems.solution: Linear: 20 s. n log n: ratio (10⁵ · 16.6)/(10⁴ · 13.3) = 12.5, so about 25 s. Quadratic: 100 times, 200 s.

problems.q: A dynamic array grows by a factor of 1.5 instead of 2. Is the amortized cost of append still O(1)?
problems.solution: Yes. The sizes at which copying occurs form a geometric series with ratio 1/1.5, so the total copying is at most n(1/(1 − 2/3)) = 3n, a constant per append. Any constant growth factor greater than 1 gives O(1) amortized, with a larger constant for smaller factors.

problems.q: The brute-force search over all subsets of m features for the best regression model takes how many model fits? If one fit takes 1 ms, how long for m = 40?
problems.solution: There are 2^m − 1 non-empty subsets. For m = 40: 2⁴⁰ ≈ 1.1 × 10¹², so 1.1 × 10⁹ seconds ≈ 35 years.
